subject: maths
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: If X ~ B(50, 0.4), what is the variance Var(X)?
questions.explain: Variance = np(1-p) = 50 x 0.4 x 0.6 = 12.

questions.q: For Z ~ N(0,1), P(-1 < Z < 1) is approximately:
questions.explain: About 68% of the standard normal area lies within one standard deviation of the mean.

questions.q: For X ~ B(12, 0.5), use symmetry: which of these probabilities equals P(X >= 8)?
questions.explain: By the symmetry of B(12,0.5) about 6, P(X >= 8) = P(X <= 4).

questions.q: A discrete uniform distribution over {1,2,3,4,5,6} has mean equal to:
For X ~ B(6, 0.5), what is P(X = 3)? (Use 6C3 = 20.)
A factory records the number of faulty bulbs in random samples of 40, each bulb independently faulty with probability 0.05. The best model is:
questions.explain: Fixed n = 40 independent trials with constant p = 0.05 give B(40, 0.05).

questions.q: For B(200, 0.5), the normal approximation N(100, 50) is reasonable mainly because:
options: n is large and np = n(1-p) = 100, both well above 5
questions.explain: With np = 100 and n(1-p) = 100, both exceed 5 and n is large, so the approximation is valid.

questions.q: For X ~ B(8, 0.25), P(X = 2) is closest to which value? (8C2 = 28.)
For X ~ N(100, 25), the standardised value of x = 90 is:
For X ~ B(10, 0.2), what is P(X = 0)?
If X ~ B(20, 0.3), what is the mean E(X)?
questions.explain: The mean of a binomial is np = 20 x 0.3 = 6.

questions.q: Heights of adult men are continuous, symmetric and bell-shaped about a central value. The most appropriate model is:
questions.explain: A continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped variable is well modelled by the normal distribution.

questions.q: For X ~ N(20, 9), the probability P(X > 20) is:
questions.explain: X = 20 is the mean, so half the area lies above it.

questions.q: If Z ~ N(0,1), then P(Z < 0) equals:
questions.explain: By symmetry about 0, exactly half the area lies below z = 0.

questions.q: X ~ N(60, 25). To find the value x exceeded by only 10% of the distribution, you use which z?
questions.explain: The upper 10% corresponds to P(Z<z)=0.90, so z = 1.28 and x = 60 + 1.28 x 5.

questions.q: X ~ N(70, 16). Which value of x has z-score exactly -1.5?
For a discrete uniform distribution on {1,2,...,n}, P(X = k) for any valid k equals:
questions.explain: Each of the n equally likely outcomes has probability 1/n.

questions.q: Which is a key property of the normal distribution N(mu, sigma^2)?
options: It can only take integer values
It is skewed to the right
It is symmetric about its mean mu
questions.explain: The normal curve is bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean mu.

questions.q: If Z ~ N(0,1) and P(Z < a) = 0.975, then a is approximately:
questions.explain: The 97.5th percentile of the standard normal is z = 1.96.

questions.q: If Z ~ N(0,1) and P(Z < a) = 0.95, then a is approximately:
questions.explain: The 95th percentile of the standard normal is z = 1.645.

questions.q: Which condition makes the normal a good approximation to B(n,p)?
options: n large with both np and n(1-p) greater than about 5
questions.explain: The normal approximation works well when n is large and np and n(1-p) are both greater than about 5 (so p is near 0.5).

questions.q: For X ~ N(mu, sigma^2), P(X < mu) equals:
questions.explain: By symmetry, exactly half the distribution lies below the mean regardless of sigma.

questions.q: In which situation is the binomial distribution NOT appropriate?
options: Number of defective items in a sample of 30 with constant defect rate
Number of red cards drawn one at a time without replacement from a deck
Number of heads in 10 coin tosses
Number of sixes in 8 rolls of a fair die
questions.explain: Drawing without replacement makes p change between trials, violating the constant-p and independence conditions.

questions.q: Which of these is best modelled by a discrete uniform distribution?
options: The score on a single roll of a fair six-sided die
The number of heads in 20 coin tosses
The number of emails per hour
questions.explain: A fair die gives equally likely integer outcomes 1-6, which is discrete uniform.

questions.q: For X ~ B(15, 0.4), which expression gives P(X >= 4)?
questions.explain: P(X>=4) = 1 - P(X<=3) since X>=4 is the complement of X<=3.

questions.q: When using a normal approximation to the binomial, P(X >= 10) is best written with which continuity correction?
questions.explain: To include X = 10 in 'at least 10', the continuity correction gives P(Y >= 9.5).

questions.q: For X ~ N(50, 16), what is the z-score of x = 58?
A fair eight-sided die has faces 1-8. The probability of rolling a value greater than 5 is:
questions.explain: Values 6, 7, 8 satisfy >5, giving 3/8 for a discrete uniform on {1,...,8}.

questions.q: For N(mu, sigma^2), approximately what proportion of data lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explain: By the 68-95-99.7 rule, about 68% lies within mu +/- sigma.

questions.q: For N(mu, sigma^2), approximately what proportion lies within two standard deviations of the mean?
questions.explain: About 95% of values lie within mu +/- 2 sigma.
